turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: “Do you need a vacation?” Wow. That was the best vacation I have ever had … in my head. A beach is much better than here. I need a vacation!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: I hear you, Anna. I need a vacation too but not at the beach. Sand is not good for robots! When we compare things, we use special forms of adjectives. "Better" is a comparative adjective. That is used to compare two things. "Best" is a superlative adjective. It shows that one thing has more of ...something than ALL of the others. Try to find more of these adjectives. Look for ER or EST at the end.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: NO! You can’t get your money back. I don’t care that it was your worst vacation ever!

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Hello! Have a seat! Welcome to the World’s Best Vacation Travel Agency!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Thank you and congratulations!

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: For what?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: For being the world’s best travel agency.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Right … thanks.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Trudy, hold my calls. I am going to sell our most expensive vacation.

turns.speaker: Trudy
turns.text: Sure thing, Boss.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: The Mountain Getaway is good for you. It’s a little pricey. But think of it -- you, on top of a mountain for seven days!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I’m afraid of high places.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Of course you are. That’s why our Deep Sea Adventure is better for you! It is pricier than the Mountain Getaway. Just you and the animals of the sea!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Shark! Shark!

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: No, there are no sharks in your dream vacation! You need the Safari Camp Out! It is our priciest vacation. But I think it’s the best one for you. During the day, you’ll see elephants, giraffes and lions. At night, you’ll sleep out under the stars.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Look, I think this was a bad idea.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Sure, you can leave. But then you won’t see the latest vacation technology.

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Did you find all of those adjectives? Dan started with good - The mountain getaway; then he moved to better - The Deep Sea Adventure. And finally, he said the Safari Campout was the best vacation for Anna!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Exactly what is the “latest vacation technology” … exactly?

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: I’m happy you asked. Meet the Travel Max 2000!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: So, tell me, how do you like to travel?

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Dan
turns.text: Great. Tell me more.

turns.speaker: Anna

Have you seen the movie “Titanic”? Oh, and no horses. But I will ride a camel. And no bike tours. Biking is THE slowest AND least romantic way to travel. Excuse me, but I think the Travel Max 2000 is on fire.

turns.speaker: Dan

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Dan

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Dan

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Don’t cry. I know what you need -- a vacation!

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Dan

turns.speaker: Professor Bot

title: Will It Float? — Touring Washington, DC
topic: Travel directions, landmarks and place prepositions
sourceLicense: VOA original public domain educational material; third-party content excluded

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Anna, thanks for taking me on a tour of D.C. today.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Sure thing, Penelope. You are new to town. And a tour is the best way to see more of the city!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: So, which tour are we taking – the one that goes through the city on a bus? Or the one that goes along the river in a boat?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Both!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: What? Anna, this isn’t going to be one of those trips, is it?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: No. Follow me.

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: In this lesson, you are going to hear lots of prepositions! What’s a preposition, you ask? It’s a word that shows relationships between things. Anna says they are going on a tour through the city and along the river. Through and along are both prepositions. Watch for more!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, Penelope, there’s our ride!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: What is it?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: It’s the famous DC Ducks -- the boat with wheels! We will ride on the road and then sail on the water!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Who thinks of these things?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I don't know. But I’m glad they do! Let’s get aboard, Sailor!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: (looking at a brochure about the boat) Hey, did you know that this bus … um, boat was created during World War II to carry people and supplies?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Wow. You know, a tour is so much more interesting with Fun Facts, like that one.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: I agree. I love Fun Facts!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Did I hear you say you love Fun Facts?

turns.speaker: Anna & Penelope
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Well, I have tons of Fun Facts for this tour!

turns.speaker: Anna & Penelope
turns.text: Great!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, where are his parents?

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Maybe - maybe he’s the Captain’s son and he helps his dad on tours!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Oh yeah! It would be so awesome to ride around the city in a boat all day with your dad!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: This is amazing, Anna. There are so many beautiful buildings along this road!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Hey, the Washington Monument is on the left!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: I have a Fun Fact too! Did you know that the Washington Monument was damaged in an earthquake? Whoa. Did you feel that?! I heard: "around the city in a boat," "along this road" and "on the left." All of these are prepositions showing place. Let's watch for more places and prepositions!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Look, Anna, we’re across from the White House!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, the only thing between us and the President is the street … and a park … and a security gate .... and police officers … with guns.

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Excuse me, do you want to know a Fun Fact about the White House?

turns.speaker: Anna & Penelope
turns.text: Yes!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Inside the White House there is a swimming pool, a movie theater and 32 bathrooms!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Thirty-two bathrooms! That’s a lot of bathrooms!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: I’d be happy with two. I live in a house with my mom, four sisters, two aunts and only one bathroom!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Oh my! You know, Anna, we should give him a tip!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Of course! It is polite to tip your tour guide! Luckily, I have lots of dollar bills!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: That was a great Fun Fact! Here you go!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Thank you! I can tell you Fun Facts all day!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Did you hear any more prepositions of place? I heard "between us and the president" “inside the White House” and "in a house." And did you hear that the Duck Boat can go on the river? I don't believe it. Join us next time to find out which preposition we will use: The boat went ON the river or The boat went INTO the river?

title: Tip Your Tour Guide — A River Tour
topic: Travel, landmarks and prepositions of place
sourceLicense: VOA original public domain educational material; third-party content excluded

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Welcome back! Anna and Penelope are taking a tour with DC Ducks. In this lesson, we are looking for prepositions. Listen for in, on, at, under and over - some important prepositions of place.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, the Lincoln Memorial is coming up on your left!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: You’re going to love my Lincoln Memorial Fun Fact!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Oh, please tell us!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: On a wall inside the memorial, the word “FUTURE” was carved wrong! They carved “EUTURE”!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, we all make mistakes.

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Yeah, but this mistake was carved in stone!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: You’re right. That is pretty bad. Here’s another dollar!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: More fun facts, please! (Crossing the river) I love riding over bridges! The water looks so pretty from here!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, this is amazing! A minute ago, we were riding along the river, and now we’re riding in the river! Awesome.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Hey, we’re passing by the Pentagon on our right!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, you love riding over the water on a bridge. But I love riding under a bridge in a boat!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Anna, look! An airplane is flying right over our heads!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Wow! This is the closest I’ve ever been to an airplane in flight. Well, I’ve been inside a flying airplane. But not outside of an airplane as it flies over my head!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: And now we’re driving out of the water. I still can’t believe this thing drives and sails!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I know. It’s amazing.

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: After we ride along these railroad tracks, you’ll see my favorite part of the tour! The U.S. Treasury where they make money!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: That young man is making a lot of money, too. Did you hear these prepositions? On your left, on our right, in the river, over bridges, over our heads, over my head, on a bridge. As you watch more, look for 'inside' and 'outside.'

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Look, the U.S. Capitol is coming up!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: I have a great Fun Fact about the U.S. Capitol.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: What is it?

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: There are tunnels under the Capitol. They connect the Capitol and office buildings of lawmakers.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I bet they built them years ago for secret reasons!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: No. The lawmakers did not want to walk around outside in bad weather.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Oh.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: We’re back at Union Station!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Do you want to know a creepy Fun Fact about Union Station? (he points to Union Station)

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: The creepier the better!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Many years ago, inside Union Station, there was a funeral home!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: A funeral home?! You mean, for dead people?!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Do you know another kind of funeral home?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: No!

turns.speaker: Boy
turns.text: Well, I’ve gotta run!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Thanks for giving us the great tour!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Captain, that was awesome! And your son is a great tour guide!

turns.speaker: Captain
turns.text: What son?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Him.

turns.speaker: Captain
turns.text: I’ve never seen that boy in my life! See ya, ladies!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: I learned many new Fun Facts in this lesson. Did you learn about prepositions? Here’s a list of all the prepositions used in this lesson. Wow! That’s a lot! I know, let’s not read them. Let’s sing them! Hit it, boys! Take it away singers!

title: The Best Barbecue — Food & Opinions
topic: Food festivals, opinions and the passive voice
sourceLicense: VOA original public domain educational material; third-party content excluded

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Thanks for meeting me.

turns.speaker: Kelly
turns.text: Sure.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I’d like to get your advice on my latest project.

turns.speaker: Kelly
turns.text: Of course. I heard you were sent to cover a big food festival that has all kinds of barbecue. So, how did it go?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, things started out great! But then, well, maybe you should watch it yourself.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: Hi English learners! Your lesson today is about my favorite food -- barbecue! Your assignment is to find passive sentences. What are those, you might ask? In passive sentences the subject receives the action! For example, “Anna was sent to cover a food festival.” Passive sentences have a form of the BE verb + the past participle of the main verb. This lesson is LOADED with passive sentences. Hey! That’s a passive sentence, too! Okay, now, it’s Barbecue Time!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Today, a Barbecue Battle is being held in Washington, D.C. This festival, which is known as one of the biggest food festivals in the United States, brings together barbecue lovers from all over the country! Barbecue is meat that is cooked over an open fire or on a grill. Chicken, pork and beef are all common meats to grill on a barbecue! No matter which meat you like to barbecue, the sauce is very important. Sauces are taken very seriously by chefs. Most ingredients are kept secret! So, can you tell us what is in your barbecue sauce?

turns.speaker: Chef 1
turns.text: No, I can’t tell you.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: So, tell us, what is the secret ingredient in your barbecue sauce?

turns.speaker: Chef 2
turns.text: (says nothing.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Sauces are made by the barbecue chefs themselves. Most sauces are made with a tomato sauce, vinegar, and spices.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: How many passive sentences did you find? Here is one I found: Today, a Barbecue Battle is being held on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Now you try. Turn this sentence from active to passive. Professor Bot loves Barbecue! Barbecue is loved by Prof. Bot. Good job! And yes, I do.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: There are some areas of the U.S. that are known for their tasty barbecue. The states of Texas, North and South Carolina and the cities of Memphis and Kansas City are known as the Barbecue Belt. People who are loyal to barbecue are really loyal to their favorite barbecue. That is why this festival is called a battle! Let’s ask a couple of people which barbecue is best.

turns.speaker: Person 1
turns.text: Texas, of course!

turns.speaker: Person 2
turns.text: Carolina barbecue is the very best.

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: Kansas City!

turns.speaker: Person 4
turns.text: Memphis style!

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: Kansas City!

turns.speaker: Person 5
turns.text: Texas!

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: Kansas!

turns.speaker: Person 5
turns.text: Texas!

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: Kansas!

turns.speaker: Person 5
turns.text: Texas!

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: I say Kansas.

turns.speaker: Person 5
turns.text: Texas!

turns.speaker: Person 3
turns.text: She keeps saying Texas, I say Kansas.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: This is Anna Matteo reporting.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Kelly, people feel so strongly about barbecue. Unbelievable! So, what do you think of my project?

turns.speaker: Kelly
turns.text: This is what I think. There is no way that Texas has the best barbecue. I am from Kansas City and we have THE best barbecue in the whole country. My mother and father owned a barbecue restaurant, which was really famous! So, I know barbecue! Anna, I know barbecue! I know barbecue! I know barbecue!

turns.speaker: Prof Bot

title: Pets Are Family, Too! — Pets and Responsibilities

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Hi Ashley!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Hey, Anna! How was your weekend?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: It was great! I went to the D.C. State Fair.

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: I would have gone, but I was busy. How was it?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: It was awesome! I won first place in a pet contest!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: But, you don’t have a pet, do you?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Yes and no. What do you mean by “pet”?

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: A pet is an animal that lives with you. People love their pets. "Ashley said, you don’t have a pet, do you? She used a tag question, a small question at the end of a sentence. Let's look for more of them!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Look, a pet! Who’s this cute little dog?

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Oh, right. You haven’t met my dog, have you? This is Dublin.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Hi, Dublin! Nice to meet you. He’s so cute!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Thanks! So, tell me about the state fair.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Oh, there were the usual things -- fair food, cute babies, music. But there must have been a dozen different contests! And some were pretty strange.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: There was a contest to see who could spit a watermelon seed the farthest. You should have seen all the people who wanted to spit a watermelon seed! And, it was pretty fun to watch. But Ashley, the pet contests were the best. There was a pet parade. Lots of people walked with their dogs.

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: That sounds so fun. But Anna, tell me, how did you win a pet contest without a pet?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Okay, the closest thing I have is my pet rock.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I know it’s silly, but I’ve had it since I was a little girl. So, for a joke, I brought it to the fair. But then I was invited to enter the “One-of-Kind Pet” contest. And I won! (holds up first place ribbon)

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Anna, only you could have won a pet contest with a pet rock. I should have brought Dublin. He would’ve won a contest!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: It’s not very easy to win one of these. (shows her the blue ribbon) Does he have a costume?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: They had a costume contest. You should have seen this little girl. She and her dog wore matching princess costumes!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Dublin doesn’t wear costumes.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Does he know any tricks?

turns.speaker: Ashley

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: You caught it, Dublin! And you killed it! Good dog! Ashley, he could have won the Best Catch contest! Aw, good boy! Ashley, pets are fun, aren’t they?

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Yes. And they become part of your family. (she drinks from her Dublin mug)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Ashley, I think I want a dog. No. I know I want a dog!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: It’s a big responsibility. You may want to spend time with a dog first.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: That is a great idea. But where can I find a dog?

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: You know, Anna, I have some shopping to do. Do you want to watch Dublin for a couple of hours?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Yes! I would! I will take very good care of him!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: I know you will. Here’s his leash.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: (to Dublin) Okay, I'll miss you!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Aw. I don’t want you to be lonely. Here, Rocky can stay with you. (puts pet rock on wall)

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Anna, I really don’t need … Okay. Thanks, Anna.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Sure. Bye, Ashley. (to Dublin) Come on, Dublin! Bye, Rocky!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Bye!

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: Anna’s rock is cute, isn’t it? Oh, there is another tag question! You found some more, didn’t you? You haven’t met my dog, have you? Go to the VOA Learning English website to learn more.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: In this lesson, you can learn about conditionals. They have "if" and "will" or "would." There are two kinds of conditional sentences in this lesson. Type 1 conditionals have a real event, and a result that probably will happen. Chances are good. Here is the pattern: If +present tense verb ... will + future tense verb. Kaveh uses this when he says: "If you ignore it, it will fly away." Type 2 conditionals have a possible event and a result that may or may not happen. We don't know. Here is the pattern: If + past tense verb ...would + infinitive verb. Kaveh uses this pattern when he says, "If all the bees died, there would be no food." Look for the "if" in a sentence to find more conditionals in today's lesson. I'll color them, too!

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Anna, Pete, I have a new assignment for you -- a show on single parents! What is it like for a mother or a father to raise a child by herself or himself?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: We can interview single parents. They can share their experiences themselves.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Yes, but you need to experience parenthood yourselves.

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Peter

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: You may be asking yourself the same thing that I’m asking myself: what is Ms. Weaver talking about!? I am sure we will find out shortly. This lesson teaches reflexive pronouns. Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject of a sentence or clause. We use them when the subject and the object are the same person or thing. For example, Ms. Weaver says, “I asked myself the same question.” “I” is the subject and “myself” refers back to it. Here, she would not use the pronoun “me.” You need to use the reflexive pronoun “myself.” Reflexive pronouns are easy to find: they end in “self” or “selves.” I have a feeling we are going to see a lot of reflexive pronouns. Listen for them!

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Here are your babies!

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: Those are bags of flour.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: No, Pete, for the next six days, this is your baby. Here are your instructions. Do not leave your babies alone. A baby cannot take care of itself. turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: (to Pete) Monster! (to Caty) This is a great idea, Ms. Weaver!

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: This is a terrible idea.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Speak for yourself, Pete! We need to throw ourselves into the research! I’m starting right now!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Come to mama!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Good girl! Good girl!

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Singular reflexive pronouns end in “self.” Plural ones end in “selves.” Anna says, “We need to throw ourselves into the research!” The subject “we” is plural. So, we must use the plural reflexive pronoun “ourselves.”

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: In Part 1 of this two-part lesson, Ms. Weaver gave Anna and Pete an assignment. Ms. Weaver instructed them to do everything by themselves. “Themselves” is a reflexive pronoun. In today’s lesson, Ms. Weaver will look at Pete’s and Anna’s research. First, let’s see Pete’s experiment.

turns.text: Okay, Pete, let me see your research first.

turns.text: Anna. Anna, you’re next. Anna? Anna wake up!

turns.text: I'm here, Baby! I’m here! I’m here! Here's your bottle.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Anna, you and your baby look awful. What happened?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, I took her everywhere. Everywhere. And I fed her every three hours. So, I haven’t slept since … what day is it?

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Okay. So, we use a reflexive pronoun when it refers to the subject of a sentence or clause. But we DON’T use a reflexive pronoun with prepositions of place. Anna uses examples of both in one sentence: While I was making myself dinner, I put Baby next to me. We use a reflexive pronoun in the first part of the sentence. “Myself” refers to the subject “I.” But in the second part of the sentence, we don’t use a reflexive pronoun in the prepositional phrase. We use the pronoun “me.” Why? “next to” is a preposition of place.

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: It was always just a bag of flour!!

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Pete, will you listen to yourself?! You sound crazy.

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: I sound crazy! This whole experiment was crazy!! She was the one who carried around and fed it and ...

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: Mmm. That is good.

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: So, what have we learned? We’ve learned when to use reflexive pronouns and when not to. Go to our website for more information! You can practice using reflexive pronouns in our comments section.

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Did you hear Ashley and Anna using the words talk and speak?

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Talk and speak both mean “to say words.” And, many times, you can use either word without losing any meaning. But there are some differences in when we use these words.

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: The word talk is usually used:

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: for conversations between two or more people

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: and informal situations, such as between friends or family

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: For example, Ashley asks Anna: “Are you talking to yourself again?”

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Speak is usually used:

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: for one-way communication, such as presentations

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: formal situations, such as a boss speaking with her workers

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: to talk about language ability

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: and in polite requests

turns.speaker: Professor Bot
turns.text: Keep watching, and listen for the words talk and speak.

turns.speaker: Anna

turns.speaker: Sue

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: The words tell and say have similar meanings. But we use them in different ways.

turns.speaker: Prof Bot
turns.text: Tell means “to inform or instruct someone with words” and is almost always followed by an indirect object. For example, Sue says, “Tell me about that.”

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: The word me is the indirect object and tells us who is being told.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: Say means “to express something with words” and focuses more on the words used. For example, Anna says, “That’s what it said. It said, ‘Use me, Anna.’”

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: Listen for when Anna and Sue use tell and say.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Hi! I see you like superhero culture. Me too.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: In fact, tonight I’m going to the big superhero convention. Are you going?

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Um, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, you'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: So, since we’re talking about superheroes: would you rather become a superhero by accident, like Spiderman, or be born a superhero, like Wonder Woman?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Take your time. It’s a big question. I thought about it for days –

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I’d rather become a superhero by an unexpected accident!

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Aren’t all accidents unexpected?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, yeah.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: What was that!? Are you okay?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I'm better than okay. I feel super!

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: Oh No! Anna was just hit by lightning. She had better get help.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: We use had better to give advice. It is very informal and stronger than should and ought to. For example, Anna says: “You'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.”

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: When we use had better, we usually shorten the word had for personal pronouns.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: We use would rather to say what we or someone else prefers to do or have. For example, the boy says: “Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

turns.speaker: Prof. Bot
turns.text: With would rather, we also shorten the word would when used with personal pronouns. Keep watching and listen for had better and would rather.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: You’d better see a doctor.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I’ve never felt better!

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: You were just struck by lightning!! And what happened to your hair and your clothes?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I don't know. Wait, I do know. This is my super suit! And this is my origin story.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: What are you talking about?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: An origin story tells the beginning of a superhero. You should know that.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: You're not making any sense, lady.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I would rather be called Lightning Bolt Lady! It’ll sound great in a theme song: Lightning Bolt Lady!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Now, I need to find my superpowers --

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Um, I really think --

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Wait. Don’t tell me. I’ll read your mind. You are thinking you’d like to be my super helper.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: I was not thinking that.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: ... that you’d like to live in a treehouse.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: … that you should eat more vegetables.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Please, stop talking. You really should get some help.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Mind reading is not my superpower. Maybe I can become invisible. I … am … invisible!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: You can’t see me. Who am I? I’m not here. You can’t see me.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: I can see you and so can everybody else.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: No power of invisibility. Maybe I can create a force field. I feel it working. Nothing can hurt –

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Someone throws a piece of paper and it hits her head.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Ow, that wasn’t very nice. I see I have a lot of work to do. Well, goodbye, non-super person!

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Wait. I’d better go with you. You might get worse…if that’s even possible.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: That's very nice of you, ordinary human. But I’d rather go by myself. This is a quest.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: Every time you speak, I get more confused.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: A quest is a part of all superhero stories. You really need to work on your superhero studies. Now, stand back. I’ve never flown before.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: And you’re not flying now.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Flying is also not my superpower. That’s too bad. It's going to be expensive to Uber everywhere. You know, I'd rather walk. It’s a nice day. Goodbye, non-super person.

turns.speaker: Young Man
turns.text: I am not talking to strangers again.

turns.speaker: Announcer
turns.text: Will Lightning Bolt Lady find her superpowers … ever? Ouch! Did that brick wall hurt? Will the young man ever talk to a stranger again?

turns.speaker: Announcer

turns.text: Let’s talk about those emergency exits.

turns.speaker: FF J
turns.text: In your home, office and schools, know where your emergency exits are located.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: What about fire extinguishers?

turns.speaker: FF J
turns.text: Everyone should know how to use a fire extinguisher. Have one handy and practice using it.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: What if we need to get out?

turns.speaker: FF J
turns.text: You should have an evacuation plan. And practice getting out safely with fire drills.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: If I am in a building and it’s on fire, should I use the elevator?

turns.speaker: FF H
turns.text: No. Always use the stairs.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: What other safety tips should I know?

turns.speaker: FF J
turns.text: Stay low. Smoke rises. The air is clearer close to the ground.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Stay low. Anything else?

turns.speaker: FF H
turns.text: If you touch a door and it’s hot, don’t open it. There might be a fire on the other side.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: What do I do if my clothes catch on fire?

turns.speaker: FF H
turns.text: Do not run. If you run, the fire will burn faster. You must stop, drop and roll.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Thanks so much! I’ve learned a lot. And I can’t wait to share this information with others.

turns.speaker: FF H
turns.text: Thanks for coming, Anna.

turns.speaker: FF J
turns.text: It’s been a pleasure meeting you.

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna is back at the office talking to Penelope.)

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: So, Anna, how was the visit to the fire station?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I learned a lot! And firefighters have a very difficult job.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Do you smell smoke?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: No. So, like I was saying, I learned how to …

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Anna, I smell smoke.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: If you smell smoke, call the fire department!

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna begins to evacuate her coworkers.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: If you smell smoke, get out of the building. Come on people, we have a fire emergency! Leave your things and evacuate calmly and quickly. Very good. Very good.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: We have a fire emergency. No, take the stairs Let’s get out. Let’s get out safely.

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna and coworkers stand outside of the building.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: We got out in less than 6 minutes! Good job, people! Wait. Where’s Pete?

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: I know where he is. I’ll go get him.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: No! Never go back into a burning building! The fire department is coming. Stay calm, Pete. Help is on the way! Help is on the way!

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Anna, where are you going in such a hurry?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Hi, Ashley. The nurse’s office. Today I get the results from my blood test.

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: I’m sure you’re fine. Don’t worry.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: You know, I used to dream of being a nurse. It is such an honorable career. Is there something you’ve dreamed of doing?

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Sure! I would love to be a dog trainer. Actually, I’ve taught my dog, Dublin, lots of tricks!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, I’m off to the nurse. Bye, Ashley.

turns.speaker: Ashley
turns.text: Bye, Anna.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Bye, Dublin.

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna stands near the nurse’s office and listens to her phone call.)

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I’m looking at her test results and they’re not good. In fact, I’m afraid she’s not going to make it.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: What?! I'm not going to make it? I'm dying??

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Anna, come in. How are you?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I guess..not so good. I’m dying!?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: What are you talking about?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I just heard you on the phone. Just tell me: How much longer do I have?

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: I wasn't talking about you. A student of mine didn’t do well on her science test. So, she won’t be able to make it ... to graduation.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Whew. Thank goodness! For a minute, my whole life passed before my eyes. There are so many things I haven't done yet.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Well, life is short. It’s important to do something you love every day.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I couldn’t agree more.

turns.speaker: Nurse
turns.text: Now, let’s talk about your blood test. Your cholesterol is really low.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Awesome!

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Next, Anna is sitting in a sound studio with Jonathan.)

turns.speaker: Jonathan
turns.text: Okay, Anna, say something and I’ll check your sound level.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Testing 1, 2, 3. Testing. Jonathan, I’ve been wondering something: What’s at the top of your bucket list?

turns.speaker: Jonathan
turns.text: That’s easy. I’d love to win the World Karaoke Contest.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: This is so strange. I just saw on Twitter that they are having auditions in D.C. this weekend!

turns.speaker: Jonathan
turns.text: Are you serious? Can you read the story by yourself?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Sure, absolutely.

turns.speaker: Jonathan
turns.text: Thanks!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: You go.

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna goes outside and talks to Penelope.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Penelope, I was wondering if you still dream of being a dancer.

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: Only every day!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, guess what: A famous dancer is having a flash mob around the corner! Hundreds of people are dancing together!

turns.speaker: Penelope
turns.text: No way!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Way! If you leave right now, you can join them! Bye!

turns.speaker: Stage direction
turns.text: (Anna then sits with Pete in the office kitchen.)

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Pete, what’s one of your dreams?

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: Well, last night I dreamt I was in a spaceship. I was flying through outer space with these two beautiful...

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Pete -- not that kind of dream. I mean your hopes for the future.

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: Oh. I plan on selling my book to Hollywood and becoming rich and famous.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: That’s going to be difficult.

turns.speaker: Pete
turns.text: It’s my agent! Hello? Uh-huh. Sure! I can be in Los Angeles tomorrow!

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Well, good job, Anna! My work here is done … almost.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: Anna, what’s going on? Where is everybody?

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: I don’t know. Maybe something is, uh, going around the office.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: You mean germs? Anna, you’d better use some of this hand cleaner. You don’t want to get sick, too.

turns.speaker: Anna
turns.text: Right. Okay, thanks. Not germs – dreams, Ms. Weaver. Dreams.

turns.speaker: Ms. Weaver
turns.text: What did you say, Anna?

turns.speaker: Anna
